name: Bilal Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew at a large mine and use an approved AI assistant to shorten the maintenance notes. I still check each detail against the radio log before I pass the page to the next shift, because a tidy summary can leave out the one warning that matters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the work, and what makes the week hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted to keep the crew moving without rushing the drivers. I earn typical pay and have about two months of expenses saved, and I send a little money to my father for his electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small AI improvement could sort the maintenance notes faster, which would help the handover. I would still compare it with the radio log and read the hazard sheet myself before putting a truck on the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker summary is useful only if it keeps the warnings in. I would say the mine should judge it by safer handovers, not by a number showing how many minutes it saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my shift is driving, so this small change does not make me expect a lost job. I have about two months saved and some mines nearby, though I still keep my father's bill in mind when I spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current truck rotation and use the assistant for notes only after checking them against the radio log. I would keep the regular transfer to savings and continue sending my father the same help each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job in this mild picture, but I still watch the household money. My father's electricity bill is predictable, and that makes it easier to hold on to the savings I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject one of the assistant's maintenance notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a radio warning or hazard-sheet note was missing, I would put the correction in before the next handover. I would ask the supervisor to check why the summary dropped it rather than quietly deciding the tool was always wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether the assistant had actually saved time without missing details?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a week of summaries with the signed radio log and count any warnings that had to be added back. If the list was complete and the crew spent less time rewriting it, I would keep that use.

say: I would use a quicker summary only if it keeps the **warnings**.
I would judge it by **safer handovers**, not minutes saved.
think: I think most of my shift is **driving**, so this change seems mild.
I remember my father’s **electricity bill** when I budget.
do: Keep my **truck rotation** and check AI notes against the radio log.
Continue savings and the **monthly help** for my father.
feel: I feel **calm** about my job, while staying careful with money.
S0.quote: I would tell the crew that a quicker summary is useful only if it keeps the warnings in.
fieldNote: Bilal already uses an approved assistant but checks **safety details manually**.
His **two-month cushion** and support for his father shape household budgeting.
He wants a **measured comparison** before expanding a tool’s use.

steps.text: Keep the truck rotation and check summaries against the radio log
Maintain the savings transfer while paying father's electricity help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side could change first: route plans, buying spare parts and writing reports. I already use an assistant for notes, so I would pay attention to whether it helps the crew or just moves more work onto the person in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the crew should learn the parts of the system that make a shift safer or clearer. I would also ask the mine to explain whether it plans to change lead hours when software takes over bookings and reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My truck work looks safer than the planning tasks, but I do not know whether the lead allowance depends on those tasks. If the company shows a real benefit and lets us practice, I can learn another feature; I do not want to spend my own savings guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the AI-drafted maintenance notes with the radio and shift logs for a few weeks. If that works, I would learn the mine's route-planning feature during a paid shift and ask the maintenance foreman about inspection training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how the lead role changes, but I do not expect the mine to replace truck drivers first. I would keep sending help to my father and postpone buying a larger television until my hours were clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sign would tell you that the new system is affecting your own pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the lead allowance on the next two pay slips and check whether our rota still names a lead operator. If either changed, I would ask the foreman whether it was temporary or part of a new staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the route planner disagreed with your judgment, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the radio, signed hazard sheet and the route itself before following it. Once the planner had been tested on that road and an experienced driver agreed, I would use it and keep a copy of the route note.

say: I would learn tools that make our shift **safer or clearer**.
I would ask whether software changes our **lead hours**.
think: I think truck work seems safer than **planning tasks** for now.
I can learn proven features without **spending my savings**.
do: Compare AI notes with the **radio and shift logs**.
Learn route planning on paid time and ask about **inspection training**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the lead role, but not about an immediate truck cut.
S1.quote: I do not want to spend my own savings guessing.
fieldNote: Bilal is already a **daily AI user** for maintenance notes.
He verifies **pay effects** before expanding his use.
He is open to training when practice time is **paid**.

steps.text: Compare AI maintenance notes with radio logs for several weeks
Ask the foreman about paid mechanical-inspection training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take over the planning and reporting by 2028, while robots reach the truck work around 2031. I would have a few years to learn what maintenance staff do, but I do not know whether the mine would keep the same number of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives first and robots follow around three years later. I would ask management to show us the training places and pay rates, because an announcement is not the same as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not much time to change trades, but I have some savings and a few nearby mines to ask. I could try a paid mechanical-inspection apprenticeship, though I would check that it teaches physical work rather than records AGI can already handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask a mechanic for one paid shadow shift each month and write down what the apprenticeship requires. In 2029, after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for a physical inspection post only if the employer named a wage and the work involved equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the mine could cut my lead duties before I finish training, even if the truck remains manual until 2031. I would hold on to my two months of savings and stop buying tools for my garage hobby until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection job is mostly records and planning that AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask whether the job includes hands-on checks or repairs, and I would ask what the pay is after the records move to AGI. There may be fewer openings than the training notice suggests, so I would not treat it as protected work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no paid inspection apprenticeship were available in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my truck job and call the nearby mines about their next paid intake. If none had an opening, I would keep saving and wait rather than leave steady wages for an unpaid course.

say: I would explain that thinking AI arrives first and robots follow **three years later**.
I would ask which training places are **actually funded**.
think: I have two years to retrain and **nearby mines** to ask.
I want physical work, not **records AGI already handles**.
do: Shadow a mechanic monthly and check the **apprenticeship requirements**.
In 2029, **apply for inspection work** only with a named wage.
feel: I feel **anxious** because lead duties could go before I finish training.
S2.quote: There may be fewer openings than the training notice suggests, so I would not treat it as protected work.
fieldNote: Bilal identifies a paid apprenticeship but questions whether it includes **physical work**.
His savings and nearby mines offer **some control**, not a guarantee.
He would delay **hobby spending** rather than leave wages for unpaid training.

steps.text: Request a paid mechanical-inspection apprenticeship intake
Stop buying garage tools until the roster and course are clear
Apply for physical inspection work with a named wage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more time to see whether a paid maintenance route is real, and robots are expected about three years after AGI. I would keep my crew job while I practiced on equipment and checked what other mines are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine should start paid apprenticeships before the planning systems change. I would not tell the crew that a three-year delay before robots means maintenance work will stay once those machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer lead could let me learn physical inspection from a mechanic who knows our fleet. AGI may still take the records and scheduling, so I would need to know whether the hands-on posts exist after 2034 and what they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the next few years to finish a paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship and keep a record of each repair I help check. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection shifts only if the employer gave me clear pay and duration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because five years gives me time to prepare, but the staffing plan is still unknown. I would keep my current wage while I learned, and I would not borrow money for a role whose future stopped at the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to pay for extra training after the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to see that the skill is used by more than one nearby mine and ask what graduates earn. If the work is mostly entering records, I would not pay extra for it because AGI can do that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if inspection shifts are few or temporary, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check vacancies at the other nearby mines and keep my haul-truck qualification active. If the only service job had no clear wage after 2034, I would keep saving and wait for a more solid opening.

say: I would ask the mine to start apprenticeships before **planning systems change**.
I would not promise the robot delay preserves **maintenance jobs**.
think: I could learn inspection from **experienced mechanics**.
I need to check whether physical jobs stay and **what they pay**.
do: Finish paid equipment-inspection training and log **repair checks**.
In 2032, **apply for inspection shifts** only with clear pay and duration.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the lead time helps, but staffing is unknown.
S3.quote: I would not tell the crew that a three-year delay before robots means maintenance work will stay once those machines arrive.
fieldNote: Bilal is willing to train while preserving his **current wage**.
He separates **hands-on inspection** from records AGI may automate.
He checks **earnings at nearby mines** before paying for advanced training.

steps.text: Finish a paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship and log repair checks
Check nearby mine vacancies before accepting short-term inspection work
Apply for physical inspection shifts with clear pay in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me room to build another skill while I keep earning a wage, and robots come about three years after the thinking change. I would use the time, but I would not assume every maintenance job survives until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell people the mine should pay workers to learn from mechanics while the work is there. I would also say it should share the likely number of jobs, because a long warning without vacancies is not much of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37, I would have time to test maintenance before AGI arrives, and I would still need a steady wage afterward. I would want to see if physical repair work has a future beyond the robot date before I put more money into training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for a paid apprenticeship and keep the savings I have instead of rushing into a private course. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would check actual maintenance vacancies and wages before I changed employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened because ten years gives me time to ask around and keep working. I would keep my current job until there was a real paid route, and I would not count a training certificate as a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before taking a maintenance post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the job pays, whether the work is mostly physical, and how long the employer expects to need people. I would want those answers before giving up the truck wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the employer cannot say whether the job will last beyond 2039, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay in the truck job while it was there and ask other mines about their training routes. If a post was only a short bridge, I would make sure the wage covered my bills before leaving.

say: I would ask the mine to pay workers to learn from **experienced mechanics**.
I would not call a warning a plan without **vacancies**.
think: At 37, I can test a trade while **earning wages**.
I will not assume repair work lasts after **2039**.
do: Ask the mine for a **paid apprenticeship** before private study.
In 2037, compare maintenance vacancies and **wages** before moving.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but ten years lets me prepare without leaving now.
S4.quote: I would also say it should share the likely number of jobs, because a long warning without vacancies is not much of a plan.
fieldNote: Bilal uses the longer lead to **test maintenance** while earning.
He wants actual **hiring numbers and wages** before changing jobs.
He sees training as preparation, not a guarantee of work after **2039**.

steps.text: Ask the mine about paid maintenance apprenticeships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is short notice to move into another trade. A paid apprenticeship, clear wages and a real vacancy list would help me decide whether maintenance is worth pursuing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A safety decision still needs someone who knows the road and the machine. I use the AI assistant for notes, but I want authority to stop when its summary and the radio log disagree.

headlineQuote: A safety decision still needs someone who knows the road and the machine.
portrait: Bilal Fischer is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
He earns typical pay, has about **two months** of expenses saved and supports his father.
Some nearby mines give him **other employers** to ask about.
He uses an approved AI assistant **daily** but verifies its notes against radio logs.
He would learn through **paid apprenticeships**, while checking wages and openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to move from lead tasks into paid training.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, clear wages and a real vacancy list would help Bilal decide whether to train.
